The Battle of Bosworth Field. On the twenty-second of August, fourteen eighty-five, a battle near the village of Bosworth in Leicestershire ended decades of civil war and fundamentally reshaped the English crown. Henry Tudor led the Lancastrian and allied forces against Richard III, the last Plantagenet king defending the Yorkist throne.

Richard III died on that field—accounts suggest he was killed charging Henry Tudor himself. He was stripped and discarded, his body left in the mud, a symbolic end to the Plantagenet line that had ruled England for over three centuries. Henry Tudor claimed the crown as Henry VII and crowned himself on the battlefield itself. He then married Elizabeth of York, uniting the warring factions through matrimony and law. The Wars of the Roses, which had torn England apart for three decades, were finally over.

But more than just a dynastic change occurred at Bosworth. The decisive moment came through a crucial defection—the Stanley family unexpectedly withdrew their support from Richard at the moment of battle, tipping the balance entirely. With this victory, Henry VII restored central royal authority and initiated a period of relative stability and cultural growth that would transform England. He founded the Tudor dynasty, which would produce Elizabeth I and eventually make England a global power. Bosworth marked a threshold, not just in English politics, but in history itself—the end of feudal medieval England and the rise of the Tudor age.
